 SCHD ETF Overtakes Vig as Best Performing Dividend ETF in 2026 
 SCHD ETF Overtakes Vig as Best Performing Dividend ETF in 2026
 Author:
 Ethan Vale 
 Reviewed by:
 EBC Research & Review Team 
 Published on: 2026-11-16 
 Updated on: 2026-11-16 
 SCHD

 The Schwab U.S. Dividend Equity ETF (SCHD) delivered a 34.7% year-to-date total return through November 13, 2026, outperforming the Vanguard Dividend Appreciation ETF (VIG) by 18.8 percentage points. Five holdings accounted for approximately one-third of SCHD’s gains, with Texas Instruments, UnitedHealth, ConocoPhillips, Chevron and Merck making the largest reported contributions. Their gains increased the value of SCHD’s underlying portfolio , supporting its substantial asset growth.
 Investor demand added another dimension to the rally. SCHD attracted $27.5 billion in net inflows during 2026, compared with $1.2 billion for VIG, as its portfolio benefited from gains in semiconductors, healthcare and energy. Portfolio appreciation and fresh capital expanded its assets, clearly strengthening its position among major dividend ETFs.
 Key Takeaways 
 2026 performance: SCHD returned 34.7% through November 13, exceeding VIG’s 15.9% and VOO’s 11.4%.
 Five major contributors: Texas Instruments, UnitedHealth, ConocoPhillips, Chevron and Merck generated approximately 11.9 percentage points of SCHD’s reported return.
 Investor inflows: SCHD attracted $27.5 billion, approximately $26.3 billion more than VIG, supporting its asset growth alongside portfolio appreciation.
 Portfolio positioning: Consumer staples, healthcare and energy represented approximately 53.7% of SCHD’s assets, giving the fund substantial exposure outside the largest technology stocks.
 Long-term perspective: SCHD’s exceptional 2026 returns narrowed its historical performance gap with VIG, while concentration and sector exposure remain important risks.
 SCHD’s 34.7% Return Outpaced VIG by 18.8 Percentage Points 
 SCHD’s 2026 advance substantially exceeded the performance of other widely followed equity ETFs. Through November 13, the fund returned 34.7%, including reinvested dividends, compared with 15.9% for VIG and 11.4% for the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF (VOO). The difference reflected strong appreciation in SCHD’s underlying holdings, along with dividend distributions.

 Different sector exposures contributed to the performance gap. SCHD benefited from energy and healthcare holdings, alongside semiconductor manufacturer Texas Instruments, while VIG’s dividend-growth strategy produced a different portfolio composition. The resulting returns illustrate how dividend-focused funds can perform differently when their underlying companies face contrasting market conditions.
 SCHD’s results were strong even within the dividend ETF category. The iShares Core Dividend ETF (DIVB) returned 37.2% over the same period, exceeding SCHD’s 34.7% gain. SCHD therefore demonstrated substantial relative strength without outperforming every dividend-focused strategy.
 Five Holdings Generated About a Third of SCHD’s Gains 
 Five companies drove SCHD’s performance, contributing about 11.9 percentage points to its reported 34.7% return. Their combined contribution accounted for 34.3% of the fund’s annual gains, showing how individual holdings shaped the outcome. These contributors spanned semiconductors, healthcare and energy, rather than reflecting gains concentrated in a single industry.
 Texas Instruments Led With a 3.8-Percentage-Point Contribution 
 Texas Instruments was SCHD’s largest reported return contributor, adding approximately 3.8 percentage points as its shares advanced 79% during the measured period. The analogue and embedded-chip manufacturer gave SCHD exposure to technology beyond the largest AI-focused chipmakers. Its contribution shows how a dividend-oriented portfolio can benefit from semiconductor gains without depending primarily on companies at the centre of the AI investment boom.
 Healthcare also contributed substantially. UnitedHealth added approximately 2.3 percentage points after joining SCHD during the March index reconstitution, while Merck contributed another 1.8 points. Together, they reinforced healthcare’s importance to SCHD’s performance during the year.
 Energy Holdings Contributed Another 4 Percentage Points 
 ConocoPhillips and Chevron generated approximately 2.1 and 1.9 percentage points, respectively. Their shares advanced around 55% and 48% during the reporting period, making energy a major source of SCHD’s outperformance. These gains also demonstrate how energy exposure can influence the returns of an ETF primarily associated with dividend income and financial quality.

 These reported contributions depend on portfolio weights and holding periods, particularly when companies enter the fund during scheduled index reviews. The figures explain a substantial portion of SCHD’s historical performance but do not establish that every holding generated positive returns. They also cannot determine whether the same companies will remain its strongest contributors.
 How SCHD’s Returns and $27.5 Billion in Inflows Expanded Its Assets 
 SCHD’s asset growth reflected two measurable developments: appreciation in its underlying holdings and substantial new investor capital. The fund recorded approximately $27.5 billion in net inflows through November 13, compared with $1.2 billion for VIG and $8.9 billion for the Capital Group Dividend Value ETF (CGDV). SCHD consequently attracted more than three times CGDV’s reported inflows and approximately 23 times VIG’s.

 Portfolio Appreciation and New Capital Supported Asset Growth 
 An ETF’s assets can expand through appreciation in its underlying investments and additional investor capital. SCHD benefited from both developments during 2026, with its 34.7% total return reflecting substantial portfolio gains while $27.5 billion in net inflows added capital to the fund. Separating their exact dollar contributions requires consistent opening asset values, cash-flow timing and adjustments for distributions.
 SCHD’s expansion also showed up in industry asset comparisons. At approximately $124 billion in assets against VIG’s $118 billion, SCHD moved ahead in ETF.com’s November comparison, although other databases reported different relative positions. These figures support SCHD’s growth but do not establish undisputed leadership across every dividend ETF classification.
 Inflows demonstrate investor demand but do not identify the motivations behind individual allocations. Dividend income, diversification and lower exposure to growth stocks are possible considerations, although aggregate flow data cannot establish their relative importance. ETF inflows also do not directly determine share prices, which primarily reflect underlying portfolio values.
 How SCHD’s Dividend Strategy Shaped Its 2026 Performance 
 SCHD tracks the Dow Jones U.S. Dividend 100 Index, which selects established dividend-paying companies using income and financial-strength criteria. Eligible companies generally need at least ten consecutive years of dividend payments before undergoing screening based on dividend yield, cash flow relative to debt, return on equity and five-year dividend growth. These requirements favour companies with established distributions and supporting financial characteristics.
 This approach contributed to SCHD’s exposure across consumer staples, healthcare, energy and information technology. As of November 13, consumer staples accounted for approximately 20.2% of assets, healthcare 18.5%, energy 15.0% and information technology 12.4%. The first three sectors represented a combined 53.7%, giving the fund substantial exposure to industries outside the largest technology-stock concentrations.
 VIG follows the S&P U.S. Dividend Growers Index, which requires companies to have increased dividends for at least ten consecutive years. It excludes the highest-yielding quarter of eligible stocks, creating a different selection emphasis. VIG therefore prioritises sustained dividend increases, while SCHD combines dividend yield with financial-quality screening.
 These methodological differences help explain why the funds posted contrasting returns in 2026. Sector exposures and individual stock performance accounted for far more of their performance gap than operating costs. SCHD’s annual expense ratio was 0.06%, compared with VIG’s 0.04%, leaving a difference of just two basis points.
 SCHD’s 2026 Gains Come With Concentration Risks 
 The same holdings that supported SCHD’s exceptional returns also created exposure to potential reversals. Its ten largest positions represented approximately 41.3% of assets on October 31, compared with a reported category average of 32.1%. This concentration gives major holdings considerable influence over fund performance when their share prices change substantially.
 Energy companies remain sensitive to commodity prices, while healthcare businesses face regulatory, reimbursement and profitability risks. Technology holdings can also experience valuation changes as earnings expectations and investment demand shift. SCHD’s dividend-quality criteria provide a consistent selection framework, but they cannot eliminate company-specific losses or guarantee future dividend payments.
 Longer-Term Returns Show a Narrower Gap With VIG 
 SCHD’s unusually strong 2026 performance should also be assessed against longer investment periods. Over five years, its reported cumulative total return reached approximately 63%, compared with 65% for VIG and 73% for VOO. The ten-year comparison showed SCHD gaining 259%, against 262% for VIG and 309% for VOO.

 SCHD’s exceptional annual performance narrowed its longer-term gap with VIG but did not establish a lasting advantage. VOO delivered higher cumulative returns over both measured periods, reflecting the different outcomes produced by broader market exposure. Future comparisons will continue to depend on sector leadership, corporate earnings and valuation changes.
